latin: Qui coniunxerit Astrologiam Cabalae uidebit quod sabbatizare et quiescere conuenientius fit post Christum die dominico, quam die sabbati.
translation: Whoever joins astrology to the Kabbalah will see that, after Christ, it is more fitting to keep sabbath and rest on the Lord's day than on the day of the Sabbath.
translation_note: 'die dominico' = Sunday, 'die sabbati' = Saturday, and no interpretive note on this thesis was located in the sources consulted (farmer1998:14180; see not_established).
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-swarm-batch4, from Latin at farmer1998:14180
doctrine: The thesis holds that joining astrology to the Kabbalah shows that, since Christ, it is more fitting to keep Sabbath rest on Sunday (the Lord's day) than on Saturday, and no interpretive note on this thesis, on any link to specific sefirot, or on alternative readings of it was located in the sources consulted, this uploaded copy of Farmer 1998 giving only the bare Latin and English of the thesis at this point, with no attached note (farmer1998:14180; farmer1998:14205; see not_established).
context: Akopyan cites the thesis as part of a sequence of Cabalistic-astrological conclusions concerning Christ, immediately after his citation of the thesis on the moon/sun correspondence of Solomon and the Messiah (11>51) (akopyan2021:3247). Elsewhere, in a note on planetary day-associations, Akopyan quotes Roger Bacon as having written, without hesitation, that Christians err by not resting on Saturday and instead working 'in the manner of the Jews' (ritu Iudaeorum), since Saturday is the day of Saturn, a planet judged 'not very fitting and fortunate' (parum commoda et felix) for undertaking affairs: 'Rogerius Bacon eo usque est evectus, ut scribere non dubitaverit errare Christianos, qui die sabbati non ferientur et operibus vacent ritu Iudaeorum, cum sit ea dies Saturni, quae stella rebus agendis parum commoda et felix existimatur' (akopyan2021:5302, quoting Bacon).
historiography: Akopyan is the principal source discussing this thesis, citing it across two studies as evidence of Pico's association of astrology with Kabbalistic and Christian symbolism of the days of the week (akopyan2018:695; akopyan2021:1451; akopyan2021:3247; akopyan2021:5302). A separate quotation attributed by Wirszubski to 'Conclusio xviii' in the excerpt available corresponds instead to the Latin of thesis 9>18, on the 'horizon of eternity and time' being proper to the Kabbalah, and is therefore not used here as evidence for 11>18 (wirszubski1989:9918).

quotations.text: Rogerius Bacon eo usque est evectus, ut scribere non dubitaverit errare Christianos, qui die sabbati non ferientur et operibus vacent ritu Iudaeorum, cum sit ea dies Saturni, quae stella rebus agendis parum commoda et felix existimatur.

not_established: No external, non-Pico source for the thesis is identified in the sources consulted; only Pico's own related theses are cited.
How Akopyan relates Roger Bacon's claim about Saturday to Pico's own conclusion about Sunday: not established from the excerpt consulted.
Whether the thesis is meant literally (calendar days) or symbolically (via sefirotic correspondences), as Farmer's note leaves open: not established by the sources consulted.
Any commission or Apologia reception of this thesis: not established by the sources consulted.

On verification against this session's uploaded copy of Farmer 1998, that phrase does not appear anywhere in the file, and this uploaded copy in fact carries no interpretive note at all for thesis 11>18 (only its bare Latin and English text, at farmer1998:14180 and farmer1998:14205 respectively). Removed as unverifiable/likely fabricated.
